title: Sudoku by unavoidable sets
description: sudoku-unique with a stronger refinement and a loop that asks for more of them. The interface holds the solved grid and the clue cells. A counterexample is a second grid that agrees with the candidate's grid on the clue cells; the cells where the two differ form an unavoidable set, and the clause "the grid changes there, or one of these cells becomes a clue" holds for every grid with the same values there, not only for the candidate's. Per candidate the loop asks for up to 3 such sets, each disjoint from the earlier ones (fix/2 assumptions). This reaches 22 clues in about 13 s, where sudoku-unique's loop does not finish k = 23 in 120 s. 20 clues stay out of reach in 5 minutes. Asking C for the smallest set (#minimize and C.solve(..., optimal)) gives shorter clauses but costs more than it saves.

fragments.name: shared
fragments.description: The size of the puzzle and the derived domains. Added to every solver.
fragments.text:
% A 9 x 9 Sudoku: every row, every column and each of the nine 3 x 3 boxes contains the
% values 1..9 once. An instance may print clues pre(R,C,V) and may fix the solved grid with
% solution(R,C,V) (Instances tab).
row(1..9). col(1..9). val(1..9).
box(R,C,(R-1)/3*3+(C-1)/3) :- row(R), col(C).
printed(R,C) :- pre(R,C,_).

fragments.name: sudoku
fragments.description: The rules of the puzzle for any grid; used by solver A (one grid) and solver C (two grids).
fragments.text:
% The rules of the puzzle, for every grid G that a solver declares with grid(G):
% cell(G,R,C,V) says that grid G has the value V in row R, column C.
1 { cell(G,R,C,V) : val(V) } 1 :- grid(G), row(R), col(C).
:- cell(G,R,C1,V), cell(G,R,C2,V), C1 < C2.
:- cell(G,R1,C,V), cell(G,R2,C,V), R1 < R2.
:- cell(G,R1,C1,V), cell(G,R2,C2,V), box(R1,C1,B), box(R2,C2,B), (R1,C1) < (R2,C2).
% Every grid respects the printed clues.
:- grid(G), pre(R,C,V), not cell(G,R,C,V).

fragments.name: abstraction
fragments.description: Proposes candidates (solver A): a solved grid and k of its cells as clues.
fragments.text:
% A candidate: a solved grid s and k of its cells that are revealed as clues.
% The grid is the instance's solution/3 if it gives one (then the grounder fixes it, which
% makes every solve call cheaper), otherwise any grid.
fixed :- solution(_,_,_).
grid(s) :- not fixed.
cell(s,R,C,V) :- solution(R,C,V).
:- fixed, pre(R,C,V), not solution(R,C,V).
k { clue(R,C) : row(R), col(C), not printed(R,C) } k.
% given(R,C,V): the puzzle shows the value V in row R, column C.
given(R,C,V) :- clue(R,C), cell(s,R,C,V).
#show given/3.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.description: The interface atoms: the solved grid and the clue cells.
fragments.text:
% The interface: the candidate's grid and its clue cells (not only the clues' values).
glue(cell(s,R,C,V)) :- row(R), col(C), val(V).
glue(clue(R,C)) :- row(R), col(C), not printed(R,C).

fragments.name: check
fragments.description: Looks for a second grid that agrees with the candidate grid on the clue cells (solver C); the cells where they differ form an unavoidable set.
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: a second grid b that agrees with the candidate's grid s on every
% clue cell. The cells D where they differ form an unavoidable set of s: in every unit,
% s and b hold the same values on D. So any grid that has s's values on D can swap them
% for b's, and a puzzle on such a grid needs a clue in D.
grid(b).
:- clue(R,C), cell(s,R,C,V), not cell(b,R,C,V).
moved(R,C) :- cell(s,R,C,V), not cell(b,R,C,V).
:- not moved(_,_).
% fix(R,C): the loop asks b to keep s's value in these cells, to find a second set that
% is disjoint from the first.
{ fix(R,C) : row(R), col(C) }.
:- fix(R,C), moved(R,C).
#show moved/2.

% The clause: s changes on D, or a cell of D becomes a clue. It holds for every grid that
% has s's values on D, not only for this candidate's grid.
relevant(cell(s,R,C,V)) :- moved(R,C), cell(s,R,C,V).
relevant(clue(R,C)) :- moved(R,C), not printed(R,C).

fragments.name: view
fragments.description: A domain view (Observatory tab): the scene part draws what stays, the frame part one step, as draw/1 marks.
fragments.text:
% The grid of the candidate with its clue cells shaded; the unavoidable set of a
% counterexample in another colour and ringed (the cells the clause asks a clue for).
#program scene.
draw(layout(grid)).
draw(cell(R,C)) :- row(R), col(C).
draw(attr(cell(R,C), stroke, box)) :- box(R,C,B), B \ 2 == 0.
draw(attr(cell(R,C), label, V)) :- pre(R,C,V).
draw(attr(cell(R,C), fill, printed)) :- pre(R,C,_).

#program frame.
draw(attr(cell(R,C), label, V)) :- cand(cell(s,R,C,V)).
draw(attr(cell(R,C), fill, clue)) :- cand(clue(R,C)).
% A solution step lists the puzzle's shown atoms: the clues.
draw(attr(cell(R,C), label, V)) :- cand(given(R,C,V)).
draw(attr(cell(R,C), fill, clue)) :- cand(given(R,C,_)).
draw(attr(cell(R,C), fill, unavoidable)) :- cex(moved(R,C)).
draw(emph(cell(R,C))) :- lit(clue(R,C), _).
draw(note("A second grid differs only in the ringed cells, so one of them must become a clue.")) :- kind(reject).
draw(note("One solution: the puzzle is done.")) :- kind(solution).
#show draw/1.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + sudoku + abstraction
solver C = shared + sudoku + check      options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

search A:
    on candidate M:
        # Up to 3 unavoidable sets of M's grid that the clues miss, pairwise disjoint:
        # after each one, the next grid b must keep s's values on the cells found so far.
        F = []
        n = 0
        while n < 3:
            X = C.solve(assume G(M), F)
            if not X: break
            reject M with G.clause(M, X)
            n = n + 1
            for a in X.atoms(moved/2):
                for x in C.atom("fix", a.arg(1), a.arg(2)):
                    F.push(x)

instances.facts: % No printed clues and no fixed grid: any puzzle with k = 22 clues.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + sudoku + abstraction
solver C = shared + sudoku + check      options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

search A:
    on candidate M:
        # One unavoidable set (the loop with n < 1); up to 3 unavoidable sets of M's grid that the clues miss, pairwise disjoint:
        # after each one, the next grid b must keep s's values on the cells found so far.
        F = []
        n = 0
        while n < 1:
            X = C.solve(assume G(M), F)
            if not X: break
            reject M with G.clause(M, X)
            n = n + 1
            for a in X.atoms(moved/2):
                for x in C.atom("fix", a.arg(1), a.arg(2)):
                    F.push(x)

solver A = shared + sudoku + abstraction   options "--enum-mode=record"
solver C = shared + sudoku + check      options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

search A:
    on candidate M:
        # Up to 3 unavoidable sets of M's grid that the clues miss, pairwise disjoint:
        # after each one, the next grid b must keep s's values on the cells found so far.
        F = []
        n = 0
        while n < 3:
            X = C.solve(assume G(M), F)
            if not X: break
            reject M with G.clause(M, X)
            n = n + 1
            for a in X.atoms(moved/2):
                for x in C.atom("fix", a.arg(1), a.arg(2)):
                    F.push(x)

solver A = shared + sudoku + abstraction
solver C = shared + sudoku + check      options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

search A:
    on candidate M:
        # Up to 2 (not 3) unavoidable sets of M's grid that the clues miss, pairwise disjoint:
        # after each one, the next grid b must keep s's values on the cells found so far.
        F = []
        n = 0
        while n < 2:
            X = C.solve(assume G(M), F)
            if not X: break
            reject M with G.clause(M, X)
            n = n + 1
            for a in X.atoms(moved/2):
                for x in C.atom("fix", a.arg(1), a.arg(2)):
                    F.push(x)

generators.name: erased
generators.description: A random solved 9 x 9 grid (a fixed grid with its values, rows within bands, columns within stacks, bands and stacks permuted) with m random cells erased; redrawn unless the erased cells have a second completion, so the printed clues pre/3 never fix the grid.
generators.text:
% erased: a random solved grid with m cells erased, redrawn until the clues left have two completions
base(R,C,((R-1)*3+(R-1)/3+C-1)\9+1) :- R = 1..9, C = 1..9.
rmap(R,(@perm(3, (R-1)/3+1, bands)-1)*3+@perm(3, (R-1)\3+1, rows, (R-1)/3)) :- R = 1..9.
cmap(C,(@perm(3, (C-1)/3+1, stacks)-1)*3+@perm(3, (C-1)\3+1, cols, (C-1)/3)) :- C = 1..9.
full(R2,C2,@perm(9, V, vals)) :- base(R,C,V), rmap(R,R2), cmap(C,C2).
erased(R,C) :- full(R,C,_), @subset(m, 81, (R-1)*9+C, cells) = 1.
pre(R,C,V) :- full(R,C,V), not erased(R,C).
1 { alt(R,C,V) : V = 1..9 } 1 :- erased(R,C).
alt(R,C,V) :- pre(R,C,V).
:- alt(R,C1,V), alt(R,C2,V), C1 < C2.
:- alt(R1,C,V), alt(R2,C,V), R1 < R2.
:- alt(R1,C1,V), alt(R2,C2,V), (R1-1)/3 = (R2-1)/3, (C1-1)/3 = (C2-1)/3, (R1,C1) < (R2,C2).
:- alt(R,C,V) : erased(R,C), full(R,C,V).
#show pre/3.

readme:
# Project: minimal Sudoku puzzles by unavoidable sets

## Research question

How much do stronger refinements (unavoidable sets, several per check) and symmetry cut the candidates of a "fewest clues" search on 9 × 9 Sudoku?

## Baseline

The default instance with k = 22 finds its first puzzle after 1,684 candidates and 2,325 clauses (17 s). `sudoku-unique` is the weaker baseline: one clause per counterexample.

## Things to try

- Ask the check for several unavoidable sets per candidate and compare the clause counts (Statistics tab, Lifting coach).
- Lift a clause over the symmetries of the grid (digit permutations, row and column swaps within a band); compare with `sudoku-symmetry`.
- Grow k downwards: at which k does the time explode, and why?

## How to measure

Add the variants, write a suite over the instances (Campaign tab, Advanced mode), and read the instance × variant matrix; headless: `node tools/bench.mjs <id> --suite NAME --out rows.jsonl` and `node tools/report.mjs rows.jsonl`. Check every variant against the `reference` loop (or the audit) on small instances before trusting its numbers.
